one_line_reason: One human meta-analysis in healthy volunteers directly shows oral activated charcoal reduces GI drug absorption when given shortly after ingestion, the core adsorption claim behind the product.

selected.intervention: oral activated charcoal administered at varying times (0 min to 4+ h) after drug intake
selected.dose_as_stated: not stated (dose expressed only as an AC/drug ratio correlate, not a fixed amount)
selected.primary_outcome: systemic drug exposure (AUC) of a co-ingested drug
selected.why_selected: The clearest human interventional evidence of activated charcoal's core adsorption mechanism, in a meta-analysis of controlled studies in healthy (non-patient) volunteers

blockers: The evidence base is decontamination/overdose pharmacology (charcoal given within hours of a specific drug ingestion to reduce its absorption), not the chronic 'detox' or GI-comfort use most catalog activated-charcoal supplements are marketed for
No fixed oral dose is stated in the abstract (effect is reported only as correlated with an AC/drug mass ratio), complicating any label-dose mapping

handoff_pmids.note: Notes activated charcoal (with cholestyramine) decreases leflunomide half-life via interrupting enterohepatic circulation, used for acute drug-toxicity management, not an efficacy claim
Position paper on ipecac syrup for GI decontamination; activated charcoal is discussed only as an alternative/interacting decontamination measure
Review of whether gastric lavage propels poison past the pylorus; activated charcoal is mentioned as part of standard poisoning management, not the study's own intervention
Review of amitraz pesticide poisoning; activated charcoal appears only within general poisoning-management context

excluded_pmids.reason: Systematic review of taste additives for activated charcoal palatability; primary outcome is palatability/adherence, not health efficacy
Review of interventions (magnesium, sodium thiosulfate, etc.) to slow vascular calcification in CKD; activated charcoal is not the studied intervention
Cochrane review of pharmacological interventions (e.g., ursodeoxycholic acid, SAMe) for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy; activated charcoal is not a primary studied intervention
Cochrane review of interventions for cholestasis in pregnancy; activated charcoal not a primary studied intervention
Earlier version of the same cholestasis-of-pregnancy Cochrane review; activated charcoal not a primary studied intervention
Consensus panel on wound dressings; concerns topical charcoal dressings, not an oral supplement exposure
Review of pressure-ulcer wound care; describes a laboratory (non-human) test of charcoal's odor-absorbing capacity, not an oral supplement trial
Study of custodial vs non-custodial criminal sanctions; the 'Hawthorn effects' mention is the Hawthorne observer-effect concept, unrelated to activated charcoal
